opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think those two things are actually more connected than people realize at first. In an autoregressive model, variable length kind of comes for free. You just keep generating tokens until you emit an end-of-sequence token, and the context grows one token at a time. With diffusion, the standard setup is that you start from a fixed-size canvas, a block of masked or noisy positions, and you refine all of them in parallel. So right away you have to ask: how big should that canvas be? If it's too small, you truncate the answer. If it's too large, you waste compute denoising a lot of padding, and quality can suffer because the model has to learn to fill the extra space with end tokens.

The way I think about it, both problems come down to how you organize computation over the sequence. One natural answer is a hybrid, semi-autoregressive approach. You generate in blocks. Within a block you get the parallelism and global refinement of diffusion. Across blocks you move left to right, so the output can grow as long as it needs to, and you can stop when the model decides it's done. That same structure also helps with long contexts, because earlier blocks become fixed. You can cache their representations, much like a KV cache in a transformer, instead of reprocessing the entire sequence at every denoising step. Without that, a naive diffusion model pays for the full context at every step, and that's what limits scaling.

So there's a design tension. Full-sequence bidirectional denoising gives you the most flexibility: the model can revise anything, plan globally, and do things like infilling. But it's the hardest to scale in length. Block-wise or causal structure makes length flexible and context efficient, but you give up some of that global editing ability. A lot of the interesting research right now is about finding the right point on that spectrum, or making it adaptive. That could mean letting the model predict how much space it needs, insert or delete positions during generation, or choose block sizes dynamically depending on the task.

My view is that these aren't fundamental barriers for diffusion. They're engineering and modeling problems that autoregressive models solved early because the solution was built into the factorization. Diffusion models make you think about them explicitly, and that's actually an opportunity, because you can design the generation process to fit the problem instead of being locked into one token at a time.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so those are really two sides of the same coin, and I think people often conflate them when they talk about the limitations of diffusion language models.

Let me start with the variable-length piece, because that's the one that comes up most often as a criticism. With an autoregressive model, length is kind of free. You generate one token at a time, and you stop when you emit an end-of-sequence token. You never have to commit upfront to how long the output is going to be. With a diffusion model, the naive formulation is that you pick a canvas, say 1024 tokens, you fill it with noise or with mask tokens, and you denoise the whole thing in parallel. So the length is baked in before you've generated anything. That feels like a fundamental mismatch with language, where the right length of an answer is something you discover as you go.

In practice, it turns out to be less of a problem than it sounds. The way we and others have handled it, in Mercury and in the masked diffusion work that preceded it, is that the model learns to emit padding or end-of-sequence tokens as part of the denoising process. So you give it a generous canvas, and the model itself decides where the content ends, and the tail of the canvas just gets filled with padding. The model is effectively predicting the length jointly with the content. And because you have a confidence signal at every position, you can be smart about this. You can decode the parts of the sequence the model is sure about first, and that often includes "this is where the answer ends."

The other technique, which is where this starts to connect to long context, is block-wise or semi-autoregressive diffusion. Instead of one giant canvas, you generate a block of, say, 32 or 64 tokens in parallel, then condition on that and generate the next block. You get the parallelism and the bidirectional context within a block, but you regain the ability to just keep going, or to stop, at the block level. So you've recovered variable length with a very mild sacrifice in parallelism.

Now, why does that matter for scaling context? If you think about the cost structure of a diffusion model, every denoising step is a full forward pass over the entire sequence. With full bidirectional attention, that's quadratic in the sequence length, and you're doing it multiple times per generation. So if you tried to do pure one-shot diffusion over a 100K-token context, you'd be paying quadratic attention across the whole thing on every single step. That's not viable. The block-wise structure fixes this because the prompt and the previously generated blocks become a fixed prefix. You can KV-cache them exactly the way an autoregressive model does, and the expensive bidirectional part is confined to the current block. So the same mechanism that gives you variable length is what makes long context tractable.

There's a subtle tradeoff there that I think is interesting. The whole appeal of diffusion is the global, non-causal view. The model can plan the end of the sentence while it's writing the beginning. The more you shrink the block size, the more you look like an autoregressive model and the more you give that up. The larger the block, the more planning you get but the more you pay in compute and the harder the length problem becomes. So block size becomes a real design knob, and we've found that the sweet spot moves depending on the task. Code, for example, benefits from larger blocks because there's a lot of structure, matching brackets, consistent variable names, where bidirectional context genuinely helps.

The thing I'd push back on is the idea that these are intrinsic limitations of the paradigm. They're properties of the simplest version of the paradigm. Autoregressive models in 2017 also didn't have long context, and it took a lot of engineering, attention variants, KV caching, position encoding tricks, to get there. We're at a much earlier point on that curve with diffusion, and I'd expect a lot of the same ideas to transfer, plus some that are unique to diffusion, like adapting the number of denoising steps to the difficulty of the block. The fact that we can already match autoregressive quality on long-form coding tasks at five to ten times the throughput suggests the ceiling is pretty high.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re related, but they’re not quite the same problem. With variable-length outputs, the question is: how does the model decide how much text to generate? In a typical diffusion setup, you start with a fixed-size collection of noisy tokens and refine it, so the size is something you’ve already chosen. You need some mechanism for predicting that length, representing the end of a sequence, or allowing the sequence to grow.

Long context raises a different question: how efficiently can you process a lot of tokens while maintaining dependencies across them? Even if you know exactly how long the output should be, repeatedly applying a denoising model to that entire sequence can be expensive.

One way to connect the two is to generate in blocks. You can use diffusion within a block and then extend the sequence with additional blocks as needed. That gives you a way to handle variable length without refining the entire growing sequence at every step. But it introduces a tradeoff: you retain parallel generation within each block, while making the generation of successive blocks more sequential. So solving variable length doesn’t automatically solve long context, but the design choices you make for one certainly affect the other.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re related, but they’re two different issues. With variable-length outputs, the question is: how do you decide how many tokens to generate? In an autoregressive model, you have a natural mechanism—you generate one token at a time until you produce an end-of-sequence token. In a diffusion model, you typically start with a collection of noisy or masked tokens, so you’ve already made some decision about the size of that collection. You need a mechanism to predict the length, represent the end of the sequence, or allow the sequence to grow during generation.

Long context raises a different question: how efficiently can you process all those tokens and capture dependencies between them? Even if you have a good solution for choosing the output length, repeatedly running a denoising network over a long sequence can still be expensive.

Where they come together is in approaches that generate blocks or progressively extend a sequence. Those can give you a way to handle variable length while keeping each diffusion problem more manageable. But then you have to think carefully about consistency across blocks and how much ability you retain to revise earlier decisions. So I would separate the two conceptually, even though the architectural choices you make can affect both.
